title: The French Defense
subtitle: Cramped on purpose — then break the chain
summary: Black invites White to build an imposing pawn chain, then spends the whole game undermining it: ...c5 against the base, ...f6 against the head, pieces massed against d4. A lesson in why a temporarily cramped position can hold a completely coherent plan — and in living with one bad bishop.

metadata.historicalContext: Named after a Paris–London correspondence match of 1834 won by the French side with 1...e6. Its greatest interpreters — Botvinnik, Petrosian, Korchnoi, Uhlmann — shared a temperament: happy to defend a small space for twenty moves in exchange for a target that cannot run away.

rootAnnotations.title: What this lesson teaches
rootAnnotations.body: The Caro-Kann lesson showed Black refusing to create weaknesses. The French makes a bolder bargain: Black concedes space and accepts a genuinely bad bishop, and in return receives a fixed White pawn chain — a permanent target with a known address. The skill this opening teaches is chain warfare: where chains are attacked, in what order, and why the cramped side is often the one with the initiative on the queenside.

annotations.body: One square forward instead of two — and unlike the Caro-Kann's 1...c6, this pawn blocks the c8-bishop's diagonal immediately. Black volunteers the very problem the Caro-Kann exists to avoid. What could be worth that?

annotations.title: A concession made with open eyes
annotations.body: Like 1...c6, this prepares the strike ...d5 with pawn support. The price is the famous 'French bishop' — c8 stares at its own e6-pawn, possibly for the whole game. What Black buys: the e6-pawn makes the coming ...d5 rock-solid, the f8-bishop and kingside develop fast, and if White pushes e5, Black gets a fixed pawn chain to attack. The French is a bet that a target-rich position matters more than one passive piece. Know the cost before you play the opening — then stop mourning it.

The prepared challenge. White's three main answers create three different games: push past (the Advance, our main road — the purest chain lesson), trade (the Exchange), or defend with a piece (the Classical). The variations here visit the other two.

annotations.title: The chain is born
annotations.body: White claims space and locks the center: pawns on d4 and e5 point at Black's kingside, and White's natural play lives there. But a chain is only as strong as its base. The head (e5) is defended by d4; d4 will be defended by c3 — and that tail-end pawn is where Black's counterplay aims. From this moment Black's moves follow one program: attack the base of the chain.

annotations.title: The Exchange Variation
annotations.body: White dissolves the tension — and with it, Black's problem.

annotations.title: The bad bishop, pardoned
annotations.body: Look at c8: the recapture reopened its diagonal, and the one concession of 1...e6 has evaporated. The symmetrical structure promises Black effortless equality — development is easy on both sides and there is nothing to attack. Many French players are privately delighted to see this variation.

annotations.title: The Classical approach
annotations.body: White defends e4 with a piece and keeps options open — but watch how quickly the same chain appears anyway.

The attacked knight tucks behind its pawns, headed for support duty. Different door, same house: the e5–d4 chain stands, and Black's program — ...c5 at the base, pressure on d4 — applies exactly as in the Advance. Learn the structure and you have learned several variations at once.
The same base-strike as the main line — proof that French plans travel between variations because the pawn structure, not the move order, defines them.

annotations.title: Strike the base
annotations.body: The central counterattack that defines the French: ...c5 hits d4, the pawn holding the chain together. If d4 falls or trades away, e5 becomes an orphan. Note the timing — immediately, before White reinforces. Black also keeps a second lever in reserve for later: ...f6 against the chain's head. Base first, head later is the classical order, and the reason is practical: the base has fewer defenders.
White reinforces the base, extending the chain one link back. Every defender White adds is a developing move not made — the hidden cost of maintaining space.
Development and pressure in one: the knight adds a second attacker to d4. Black's pieces will keep arriving at this pawn like a queue forming.

annotations.title: The queen joins the siege
annotations.body: A third attacker on d4 — and from b6 the queen also eyes b2, tying White's dark-squared bishop to its defense. An early queen move, and a correct one: it makes concrete threats from a square where nothing can harass it. (Recall the Scotch lesson: the rule against early queens is about cost, and here the cost is zero.) The cramped side attacks — this is what French counterplay looks like.
Black cashes the c-pawn to fix d4 as a permanent target: after the recapture, no c-pawn remains to defend it, and the siege continues against a pawn that can only be defended by pieces.

The knight takes the long way — via e7 toward f5, the perfect attacking square against d4. In cramped positions, knights choose routes, not just squares; ...Nh6–f5 is the same journey by another road.

White develops and hopes to hold d4 with pieces alone. It looks defensible — count the attackers and defenders yourself before reading on. The variation at Black's next move shows why the arithmetic is a trap.

annotations.title: Three attackers and a poisoned pawn
annotations.body: Queen, knight, and knight now converge on d4 against two defenders — yet Black should not grab it: the variation shows the famous trap where winning d4 loses the queen to a discovered attack. The point of the pressure is not the pawn but the paralysis: White's pieces are chained to d4's defense while Black completes development with ...Be7 and ...O-O. A won pawn ends a siege; a permanent siege can be worth more.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three lessons: a space disadvantage is a location, not a verdict — Black's position was cramped and never passive for a single move; fixed pawn chains dictate the plans for both sides — White must play where the chain points (kingside), Black where its base lives (queenside and center); and the French bargain is honest — the bad bishop is real, and so is the target. Compare the Caro-Kann: same ...d5 strike, opposite trade-off. Two doors into the same fight for the center.

annotations.title: The pawn is poisoned
annotations.body: Winning the besieged pawn at last — and walking into one of the oldest traps in the French. Watch the sequence to the end.
Recapturing feels forced and safe — the queen even hits the e5 pawn. But White's next move reveals what the innocent bishop on e2 was really doing.

annotations.title: The discovered attack
annotations.body: A check from nowhere — and the real point is behind it: the d1-queen now stares straight at Black's queen on d4. Black must answer the check, and then White simply captures on d4. The lesson transfers everywhere: before your queen captures on a half-open file, ask what stands at the far end of it.
